newsitem.title: IRAQ: Syria takes growing share of Iraq's border trade.
newsitem.headline: Syria takes growing share of Iraq's border trade.

text.p: Syrian businessmen trying to sell goods to Iraq are finding better trading opportunities than their competitors from other countries, traders said on Wednesday.

Syrian traders, who are crowding five-star hotels in Baghdad, said that most of Iraq's border trade would shift from Jordan - Iraq's biggest trading partner since the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait - to Syria.

"I do not want to say that opening the Iraqi-Syrian border would impede trade between Iraq and Jordan, but things are going in that direction I'm afraid," Hussein Ghneim, a Syrian businessman visiting Baghdad, told Reuters.

The Syrian export drive has been helped by the two countries' decision a few weeks ago to reopen their border for trade. The border had been closed since 1980, when ties were cut because Damascus sided with Iran in the 1980-88 Iraq-Iran war.
Direct travel between the two countries, non-existent in recent years, resumed last week when two buses began a daily service between Baghdad and Damascus.
"I think the days of Jordan being Iraq's main supplier of goods are withering away. We, the private traders, are slowly switching to Syria," said an Iraqi trader who asked not to be named.
"Syria is the Arab Hong Kong. We sell our own goods, not like the Jordanians who sell imported commodities to Iraq," said Ghneim.
"We more or less look like each other (the Syrians and the Iraqis). They eat the things we like to eat and their taste in clothes is similar to ours," he said.
Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz said last June in Amman that the opening of Iraq's border with Syria would not damage Baghdad's trade with Jordan.
The Iraqi trade is vital for Jordan, which sympathised with Baghdad during the Gulf crisis caused by Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, but later turned against Iraq.
Syrian businessmen are hoping to secure most of Iraq's food and medicine contracts under the second phase of Baghdad's "oil-for-food" deal with the United Nations.
The pact allows Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy humanitarian goods to help Iraqis offset the effects of U.N. sanctions imposed after Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
During the first six-month deal, Syrian businessmen won contracts to supply Baghdad with $20 million worth of food and medical supplies.
Last Friday the United Nations approved a crossing point on the Iraqi-Syrian border as a new entry point for goods entering Iraq under the oil for food pact.

"The Syrians are willing to secure most of the Iraqi contracts under the second phase of the agreement but I expect the U.N. (sanctions committee on Iraq) to create obstacles to prevent them from doing so," Ghneim said.
Syrian traders are becoming a common sight in Baghdad, and the display of Syrian sweets, detergents and canned food in the capital's shops shows how trade is growing.
Syrian firms have exhibitions of their products here almost every week, medical equipment and clothing being among the latest.
Iraqi newspapers say Syrian firms are expected to have a significant presence at the annual Baghdad trade fair in November.
